'''''Erica cerinthoides''''' is a [[species]] of [[Heath (habitat)|heath]] native to [[South Africa]] (the [[Cape Provinces]], the [[Free State (province)|Free State]], [[KwaZulu-Natal]], the [[Northern Provinces]]), [[Lesotho]] and [[Eswatini]].<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate=2010-10-04}}</ref> Common names include '''fire erica''', '''fire heath''', '''red hairy heath''', '''rooihaartjie''' or '''klipheide'''. Throughout its range the species shows marked variation in habit, flower characteristics and hairiness. A form with white flowers is found in [[Eswatini]] and the South African province of [[Mpumalanga]] while the variety ''E. cerinthoides'' var. ''barbertona'' has shorter flowers.<ref name=plantzafrica>{{cite web|title=''Erica cerinthoides''|work=PlantZAfrica.com|url=http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantefg/ericacerinth.htm |author=Hitchcock, Anthony |year=2001|accessdate=26 November 2016}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Erica cerinthoides'' is a variable plant over different parts of its range, varying in habit of growth, the hairiness of the leaves and the flowers, and the colour, size and shape of the flowers. Where it remains unburnt it can be a straggly bush over {{Convert|1|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} tall, bare of leaves apart from a few extremities, and producing few flowers. Elsewhere it can be a compact small plant covered in blooms.<ref name="plantzafrica" />

== Etymology ==
The Latin [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''cerinthoides'' means "resembling honeywort (''[[Cerinthe]]'')".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for Gardeners |year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |location=United Kingdom |isbn=184533731X }}</ref> The flowers bear a superficial resemblance to flowers of that genus in the family Boraginaceae, though it is only distantly related.

==Distribution and habitat==
''E. cerinthoides'' is [[Endemism|endemic]] to southern Africa. Its range extends from the [[Cederberg|Cedarberg Mountains]] in the [[Western Cape]] to the [[Eastern Cape]], [[Transkei]], and [[Drakensberg]], as well as [[Mpumalanga]], Lesotho and Eswatini. Its northernmost limit is the [[Soutpansberg]] in the province of [[Limpopo]]. It grows in various habitats, from sea level to high mountains. It sprouts readily from the woody rootstock after fires which enables it to thrive when other vegetation is destroyed. Fire seems to stimulate flowering, and bushy plants of ''E. cerinthoides'' can be seen in flower against a blackened landscape.<ref name=plantzafrica/>

==Cultivation==
''E. cerinthoides'' requires a position in full sun with good drainage, and [[soil pH|acidic soil]]. It is frost sensitive, but can regrow following damage. Plants can be propagated from cuttings of current season's  growth with a heel of older wood. They can also be grown from seed.<ref name=plantzafrica/> In the [[United Kingdom|UK]] it has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web
